text: John Constable RA (/ˈkʌnstəbəl, ˈkɒn-/;[1] 11 June 1776 – 31 March 1837) was an English landscape painter in the Romantic tradition, born in East Bergholt, Suffolk, to Golding and Ann (Watts) Constable.[6] His father, a wealthy corn merchant, owned Flatford Mill in East Bergholt and later Dedham Mill in Essex, and operated a small ship, The Telegraph, moored at Mistley on the Stour estuary to transport corn to London.[7] A cousin of the London tea merchant Abram Newman, Constable was expected to succeed his father in the business, though his older brother was intellectually disabled. After brief schooling in Lavenham,[8] he attended a day school in Dedham, Essex,[9] and later worked in the corn trade, with his younger brother Abram eventually taking over the mills.[10] As a youth, he made amateur sketching trips in the Suffolk and Essex countryside, which became central to his art; he described these scenes as "making me a painter, and I am grateful," noting his love for the sounds of water, willows, rotten planks, and brickwork.[11][12] Introduced to George Beaumont, a collector, he saw Claude Lorrain’s Hagar and the Angel, which inspired him; while visiting relatives in Middlesex, he met professional artist John Thomas Smith, who advised him to remain in the family business rather than pursue art professionally. In 1799, Constable persuaded his father to allow him to pursue art, receiving a small allowance and entering the Royal Academy Schools as a probationer, where he studied life classes, anatomical dissections, and copied old masters, including works by Thomas Gainsborough, Claude Lorrain, Peter Paul Rubens, Annibale Carracci, and Jacob van Ruisdael.[14] He also read widely in poetry and sermons and became a notably articulate artist. In 1802, he refused a position as drawing master at Great Marlow Military College (now Sandhurst), a decision counselled by Benjamin West as likely to end his career, and wrote a letter to John Dunthorne declaring his intent to become a professional landscape painter, criticizing the prevailing trend of "bravura" and advocating for a truthful representation of nature.[15] His early style featured freshness of light, colour, and touch, influenced by the old masters, particularly Claude Lorrain.[16] Though his subjects—scenes of ordinary daily life—were unfashionable in an age favoring romantic visions of wild landscapes and ruins, he made occasional trips farther afield. By 1803, he was exhibiting at the Royal Academy; in April 1803, he spent nearly a month aboard the East Indiaman Coutts traveling from London to Deal and on to China.[17] In 1806, he undertook a two-month tour of the Lake District, where he told his biographer Charles Robert Leslie that the solitude of the mountains distressed him, as his nature was social and required human associations such as villages, churches, farmhouses, and cottages.[19] He established a routine of winter in London and summer painting in East Bergholt. In 1811, he visited John Fisher and his family in Salisbury, whose cathedral and landscape inspired some of his greatest works. To support himself, he took up portraiture, which he found dull, and painted occasional religious works, though John Walker noted his "incapacity as a religious painter" was "unoverstated."[20] He also received commissions for country house painting; in 1816, he painted Wivenhoe Park for Major-General Francis Slater Rebow, and a smaller work of Alresford Hall’s fishing lodge, now in the National Gallery of Victoria,[21] which he used to fund his wedding to Maria Bicknell.[21] This period featured idyllic country scenes with detailed work, including The Wheat Field (1816).[23] From 1809, his friendship with Maria Elizabeth Bicknell deepened into a mutual love; their marriage in October 1816 at St Martin-in-the-Fields (with Fisher officiating) was opposed by Maria’s grandfather, Dr. Rhudde, rector of East Bergholt, who considered the Constables socially inferior and threatened Maria with disinheritance. Maria’s father, Charles Bicknell, solicitor to George IV and the Admiralty,[24] was reluctant to see Maria sacrifice her inheritance, and Maria emphasized that a penniless marriage would harm Constable’s career. Golding and Ann Constable approved the match but offered no financial support until Constable was secure. After both died in quick succession, Constable inherited a fifth share in the family business. Following their marriage, the couple stayed at Fisher’s vicarage and took a honeymoon tour of the south coast, where the sea at Weymouth and Brighton inspired new techniques of brilliant colour and vivacious brushwork and introduced a greater emotional range to his art.[25] While on honeymoon, he began experimenting with works showing nature’s grandeur, such as Osmington Bay.[26] Three weeks before their marriage, he began work on Flatford Mill (Scene on a Navigable River), the largest working scene on the River Stour he had ever completed largely outdoors and the largest canvas of its kind.[27][28] He aimed to attract attention at Royal Academy exhibitions and project his ideas on a scale comparable to classical landscape painters he admired.[29] Although Flatford Mill failed to sell at the 1817 Royal Academy exhibition,[27] its intricate execution earned widespread praise, encouraging him to pursue larger canvases. In 1819, he sold his first important painting, The White Horse, for 100 guineas to John Fisher, marking a turning point in his career; the sale provided him with financial freedom, led to his election as an associate of the Royal Academy,[32] and prompted a series of six monumental landscapes on the River Stour known as the “six-footers” (named for their size), including Stratford Mill (1820, National Gallery, London), The Hay Wain (1821, National Gallery, London), View on the Stour near Dedham (1822, Huntington Library and Art Gallery, Los Angeles County), The Lock (1824, Private Collection), and The Leaping Horse (1825, Royal Academy of Arts, London).[30] The following year, Stratford Mill was exhibited and praised by The Examiner as having “a more exact look of nature than any picture we have ever seen by an Englishman”; it sold for 100 guineas to John Fisher’s solicitor and friend, John Pern Tinney,[35] who offered Constable another 100 guineas for a companion piece, which he declined.[35] His growing popularity led to more lucrative commissions, such as Malvern Hall (1821, Clark Art Institute).[38] In 1821, The Hay Wain was exhibited at the Royal Academy but failed to sell; however, it was viewed by French artists Théodore Géricault and Charles Nodier, with Géricault returning to France “quite stunned” and Nodier urging French artists to draw inspiration from nature rather than Rome.[39] The painting, along with View on the Stour near Dedham, was eventually purchased by Anglo-French dealer John Arrowsmith in 1824, with Yarmouth Jetty added, totaling £250; both were exhibited at the Paris Salon, where The Hay Wain won a gold medal from Charles X.[39] The Hay Wain was later acquired by Henry Vaughan and donated to the National Gallery in 1886. Delacroix wrote in his journal that Constable’s description of meadow green could be applied to every tone, and after seeing the Constables at Arrowsmith’s gallery, he repainted the background of his 1824 Massacre de Scio, which he said had greatly benefited him.[40][41] The Lock was not completed in time for the 1823 exhibition, so Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop’s Grounds was shown instead; after Fisher sent him money, the painting was completed and exhibited the following year, selling for 150 guineas on the first day of the exhibition—the only Constable painting to do so.[42][43] The Lock is the only upright landscape in the Stour series and the only six-footer Constable painted more than one version of; a second version, the “Foster version,” was painted in 1825 and kept by Constable for exhibitions; a third, A Boat Passing a Lock (1826), is in the Royal Academy of Arts collection.[44] The Leaping Horse, the only six-footer from the Stour series not to sell during Constable’s lifetime, remained unsold.[45] After Maria began showing symptoms of tuberculosis, Constable moved his family to Brighton from 1824 to 1828, hoping the sea air would improve her health,[46] splitting his time between Charlotte Street in London and Brighton. This shift led him to focus on coastal scenes, though he initially doubted Brighton’s suitability as a subject; in a letter to Fisher in 1824, he wrote that the sea’s “magnificence” was drowned by the noise of stage coaches, gigs, and “flys,” and that the beach was merely “Piccadilly by the sea-side.”[49][50] In his lifetime, Constable sold only 20 paintings in England, but sold more than 20 in France in a few years. Despite this, he refused all international invitations to promote his work, writing to Francis Darby: “I would rather be a poor man [in England] than a rich man abroad.”[20] In 1825, due to Maria’s illness, the discomfort of living in Brighton, and pressure from outstanding commissions, he quarreled with Arrowsmith and lost his French outlet. Chain Pier, Brighton was his only ambitious six-foot painting of a Brighton subject, exhibited in 1827.[51] The Constables remained in Brighton for five years, but Maria died on 23 November 1828 at the age of 41.[52] Deeply affected, Constable wrote to his brother Golding: “hourly do I feel the loss of my departed Angel—God only knows how my children will be brought up...the face of the World is totally changed to me.”[53] He then dressed in black and was described by Leslie as “a prey to melancholy and anxious thoughts.” He cared for his seven children alone for the rest of his life—John Charles, Maria Louisa, Charles Golding, Isobel, Emma, Alfred, and Lionel—only Charles Golding Constable producing offspring; several of the children also painted, notably Lionel, whose works are in the Clark Art Institute.[54][55] Shortly before Maria’s death, her father died, leaving her £20,000; Constable mismanaged the funds, paying for mezzotint engravings of his landscapes in preparation for a publication. He struggled with indecision, nearly clashed with his engraver, and the folios failed to attract subscribers. He collaborated closely with mezzotinter David Lucas on 40 prints after his landscapes, one of which went through 13 proof stages, corrected by Constable in pencil and paint; he said Lucas “showed me to the public without my faults,” but the venture was not financially successful.[56] His art evolved from serenity to a more broken and accented style, evident in later six-foot masterpieces Hadleigh Castle (1829) and Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows (1831), among his most expressive works. In February 1829, he was elected to the Royal Academy at the age of 52 and in 1831 was appointed Visitor at the Royal Academy, where he was popular with students. He delivered public lectures on the history of landscape painting, including a series at the Royal Institution in 1836, in which he proposed a three-fold thesis: first, painting is “scientific as well as poetic”; second, “that imagination never did, and never can” produce art comparable to reality; and third, “that no great painter was ever self taught.”[57] He also spoke against the Gothic Revival movement, which he viewed as mere “imitation.” In 1835, his final lecture to Royal Academy students, in which he praised Raphael and called the Academy the “cradle of British art,” was “cheered most heartily.”[58] He died on the night of 31 March 1837, apparently from heart failure, and was buried with Maria in the graveyard of St John-at-Hampstead Church in Hampstead, London. John Constable was appointed Visitor at the Royal Academy, where he was popular with students. He delivered public lectures on the history of landscape painting, attended by distinguished audiences, and in 1836 gave a series of lectures at the Royal Institution proposing a three-fold thesis: first, that painting is scientific as well as poetic; second, that imagination never did and never can produce art comparable to reality; and third, that no great painter was ever self-taught. He also spoke against the Gothic Revival movement, which he viewed as mere imitation. In 1835, his final lecture to Royal Academy students, in which he praised Raphael and called the Academy the "cradle of British art," was met with enthusiastic approval. Constable died on the night of 31 March 1837, reportedly from heart failure, and was buried with Maria in the graveyard of St John-at-Hampstead Church in Hampstead, London; his children, John Charles Constable and Charles Golding Constable, are also buried in the same family tomb. His friend Charles Robert Leslie published the influential biography Memoirs of the Life of John Constable in 1843. Bridge Cottage, a National Trust property, is open to the public, and nearby Flatford Mill and Willy Lott's Cottage (visible in The Hay Wain) are used by the Field Studies Council for courses. The largest collection of original Constable paintings outside London is displayed at Christchurch Mansion in Ipswich, and Somerville College, Oxford holds a portrait by Constable. Constable quietly opposed the artistic culture that encouraged artists to use imagination rather than nature, stating to Leslie, "When I sit down to make a sketch from nature, the first thing I try to do is to forget that I have ever seen a picture." He attributed his artistic gift to the Stour river, though biographer Anthony Bailey credited his development to the influence of his well-to-do relative Thomas Allen and the London contacts Allen introduced him to. Although Constable produced paintings for the "finished" picture market and R.A. exhibitions, constant on-the-spot studies were essential to his method, and he was never satisfied with following a formula, writing, "The world is wide, no two days are alike, nor even two hours; neither were there ever two leaves of a tree alike since the creation of all the world; and the genuine productions of art, like those of nature, are all distinct from each other." He painted many full-scale preliminary sketches to test compositions, using free and vigorous brushwork that was revolutionary at the time and continues to interest artists, scholars, and the public. The oil sketches of The Leaping Horse and The Hay Wain show greater vigour and expressiveness than the finished versions. Constable's watercolours were also remarkably free; the almost mystical Stonehenge, 1835, with its double rainbow, is considered one of the greatest watercolours ever painted, and when exhibited in 1836, he added the text: "The mysterious monument of Stonehenge, standing remote on a bare and boundless heath, as much unconnected with the events of past ages as it is with the uses of the present, carries you back beyond all historical records into the obscurity of a totally unknown period." In addition to full-scale oil sketches, he made numerous observational studies of landscapes and clouds, aiming to record atmospheric conditions scientifically. The power of his physical effects was evident in works like The Chain Pier, 1827, which prompted a critic to note the "characteristic humidity" that evoked a desire for an umbrella. His oil sketches were among the first done directly from nature in the open air, with the notable exception of Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes' work in Rome around 1780. To capture light and movement, he used broken brushstrokes, often in small touches, scumbled over lighter areas to create a sense of sparkling light. One of his most expressionistic studies, Seascape Study with Rain Cloud (painted about 1824 at Brighton), captures the immediacy of an exploding cumulus shower with slashing dark brushstrokes. He also explored rainbow effects, as seen in Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows, 1831, and Cottage at East Bergholt, 1833. To his sky studies, he added notes on the back detailing weather, direction of light, and time of day, believing the sky to be "the key note, the standard of scale, and the chief organ of sentiment" in landscape painting. He was influenced by meteorologist Luke Howard's work on cloud classification, as shown in his annotations of Thomas Forster's Researches About Atmospheric Phaenomena. He wrote to Fisher on 23 October 1821, "I have done a good deal of skying; I am determined to conquer all difficulties, and that most arduous one among the rest." In a letter to Leslie, he stated, "My limited and abstracted art is to be found under every hedge, and in every lane, and therefore nobody thinks it worth picking up." He could not have imagined how influential his honest techniques would become, as his work inspired contemporaries like Géricault and Delacroix, the Barbizon School, and the French impressionists of the late nineteenth century. In 2019, two drawings by Constable were discovered among the possessions of Christopher Fry and later sold for £60,000 and £32,000 at auction.
